knowledge_cards.fact_statement: Penicillin is used to treat streptococcal meningitis.
knowledge_cards.source_span: Fleming first used the purified penicillin to treat streptococcal meningitis in 1942.

knowledge_cards.fact_statement: Penicillin can be used to treat neonatal conjunctivitis.
knowledge_cards.source_span: Cecil George Paine was the first to successfully use penicillin to treat eye infection (neonatal conjunctivitis) in 1930.

knowledge_cards.fact_statement: Penicillin G is licensed for the treatment of pneumonia.
knowledge_cards.source_span: Penicillin G is licensed for use to treat septicaemia, empyema, pneumonia, pericarditis, endocarditis and meningitis

knowledge_cards.fact_statement: Penicillin G is licensed to treat endocarditis.
knowledge_cards.source_span: Penicillin G is licensed for use to treat septicaemia, empyema, pneumonia, pericarditis, endocarditis and meningitis

knowledge_cards.fact_statement: Penicillin G is licensed for the treatment of anthrax.
knowledge_cards.source_span: It is also licensed for the treatment of anthrax, actinomycosis, cervicofacial disease

knowledge_cards.fact_statement: Penicillin G is used as an adjunctive therapy to treat tetanus.
knowledge_cards.source_span: tetanus (as an adjunctive therapy to human tetanus immune globulin)

knowledge_cards.fact_statement: Penicillin G is licensed to treat syphilis.
knowledge_cards.source_span: meningococcal meningitis and/or septicaemia caused by penicillin-susceptible organisms and syphilis.

knowledge_cards.fact_statement: Penicillin kills bacteria by inhibiting the synthesis of peptidoglycans.
knowledge_cards.source_span: Penicillin kills bacteria by inhibiting the completion of the synthesis of peptidoglycans, the structural component of the bacterial cell wall.

knowledge_cards.fact_statement: Penicillin functions by binding to penicillin binding proteins.
knowledge_cards.source_span: It does this by binding to penicillin binding proteins with the β-lactam ring, a structure found on penicillin molecules.

knowledge_cards.fact_statement: Penicillin inactivates the enzyme DD-transpeptidase.
knowledge_cards.source_span: As a consequence, DD-transpeptidase is inactivated, the formation of cross-links between UDP-MurNAc and N-acetyl glucosamine is blocked

knowledge_cards.fact_statement: Penicillin causes cell lysis in bacteria.
knowledge_cards.source_span: This results in cell lysis and death.

knowledge_cards.fact_statement: Penicillin triggers the activation of bacterial cell wall hydrolases.
knowledge_cards.answer: activation of bacterial cell wall hydrolases
knowledge_cards.source_span: the build-up of peptidoglycan precursors triggers the activation of bacterial cell wall hydrolases and autolysins

knowledge_cards.fact_statement: Penicillin acts as an analogue of D-alanine-D-alanine.
knowledge_cards.source_span: Penicillin and other β-lactam antibiotics act as an analogue of D-alanine-D-alanine (the dipeptide) in UDP-MurNAc

knowledge_cards.fact_statement: A common adverse drug reaction associated with penicillin is diarrhoea.
knowledge_cards.source_span: Common (≥ 1% of people) adverse drug reactions associated with use of the penicillins include diarrhoea

knowledge_cards.fact_statement: Nausea is a common adverse effect of penicillin.
knowledge_cards.source_span: Common (≥ 1% of people) adverse drug reactions associated with use of the penicillins include diarrhoea, hypersensitivity, nausea

knowledge_cards.fact_statement: Penicillin use can result in neurotoxicity.
knowledge_cards.source_span: Common (≥ 1% of people) adverse drug reactions associated with use of the penicillins include diarrhoea, hypersensitivity, nausea, rash, neurotoxicity

knowledge_cards.fact_statement: Infrequent adverse effects of penicillin include seizures.
knowledge_cards.source_span: Infrequent adverse effects (0.1–1% of people) include fever, vomiting, erythema, dermatitis, angioedema, seizures

knowledge_cards.fact_statement: Penicillin can cause pseudomembranous colitis as an infrequent side effect.
knowledge_cards.source_span: Infrequent adverse effects (0.1–1% of people) include fever, vomiting, erythema, dermatitis, angioedema, seizures (especially in people with epilepsy), and pseudomembranous colitis.

knowledge_cards.fact_statement: Penicillin can induce serum sickness in some individuals.
knowledge_cards.source_span: Penicillin can also induce serum sickness or a serum sickness-like reaction in some individuals.

knowledge_cards.fact_statement: Penicillin is originally obtained from Penicillium rubens.
knowledge_cards.source_span: originally obtained from Penicillium moulds, principally P. chrysogenum and P. rubens.

knowledge_cards.fact_statement: Most penicillins in clinical use are synthesised by Penicillium chrysogenum.
knowledge_cards.source_span: Most penicillins in clinical use are synthesised by P. chrysogenum

knowledge_cards.fact_statement: Penicillin is produced using deep tank fermentation.
knowledge_cards.source_span: synthesised by P. chrysogenum using deep tank fermentation and then purified.

knowledge_cards.fact_statement: Penicillin G is produced when corn steep liquor is used as the culture medium.
knowledge_cards.source_span: produces penicillin G as the principal component when corn steep liquor is used as the culture medium.

knowledge_cards.fact_statement: Penicillins are a group of β-lactam antibiotics.
knowledge_cards.source_span: Penicillins (P, PCN or PEN) are a group of β-lactam antibiotics

knowledge_cards.fact_statement: Penicillin contains a thiazolidine ring fused to its core.
knowledge_cards.source_span: contains a thiazolidine ring fused to the β-lactam core

knowledge_cards.fact_statement: The common core skeleton of penicillins is described by the term penam.
knowledge_cards.source_span: The term "penam" is used to describe the common core skeleton of a member of the penicillins.

knowledge_cards.fact_statement: Penicillin was discovered by Alexander Fleming.
knowledge_cards.source_span: Penicillin was discovered in 1928 by the Scottish physician Alexander Fleming

knowledge_cards.fact_statement: The purified compound of penicillin was isolated by a research team led by Howard Florey and Ernst Boris Chain.

knowledge_cards.fact_statement: Decreased or absent insulin activity results in diabetes.
knowledge_cards.source_span: Decreased or absent insulin activity results in diabetes

knowledge_cards.fact_statement: In type 1 diabetes, insulin can no longer be synthesized due to the destruction of beta cells.
knowledge_cards.source_span: In type 1 diabetes, the beta cells are destroyed by an autoimmune reaction so that insulin can no longer be synthesized

knowledge_cards.fact_statement: Insulin resistance is known to be involved in the pathogenesis of type 2 diabetes.
knowledge_cards.source_span: The pathogenesis of type 2 diabetes is not well understood but reduced population of islet beta-cells, reduced secretory function of islet beta-cells that survive, and peripheral tissue insulin resistance are known to be involved.

knowledge_cards.fact_statement: A lack of insulin activity causes a condition of high blood sugar level known as hyperglycaemia.
knowledge_cards.source_span: Decreased or absent insulin activity results in diabetes, a condition of high blood sugar level (hyperglycaemia).

knowledge_cards.fact_statement: Insulin promotes the absorption of glucose from the blood into cells.
knowledge_cards.source_span: promoting the absorption of glucose from the blood into cells of the liver, fat, and skeletal muscles.

knowledge_cards.fact_statement: Insulin inhibits gluconeogenesis in the liver.
knowledge_cards.source_span: glucose production by the liver through glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis are inhibited.

knowledge_cards.fact_statement: Insulin induces the formation of glycogen.
knowledge_cards.source_span: Induced glycogen synthesis – When glucose levels are high, insulin induces the formation of glycogen

knowledge_cards.fact_statement: Insulin decreases lipolysis in fat cells.
knowledge_cards.source_span: Decreased lipolysis in – forces reduction in conversion of fat cell lipid stores into blood fatty acids and glycerol

knowledge_cards.fact_statement: Insulin decreases proteolysis by reducing the breakdown of protein.
knowledge_cards.source_span: Decreased proteolysis – decreasing the breakdown of protein

knowledge_cards.fact_statement: Insulin decreases autophagy, lowering the degradation of damaged organelles.
knowledge_cards.source_span: Decreased autophagy – decreased level of degradation of damaged organelles.

knowledge_cards.fact_statement: Insulin forces cells to absorb circulating amino acids.
knowledge_cards.source_span: Increased amino acid uptake – forces cells to absorb circulating amino acids

knowledge_cards.fact_statement: Medications used to treat diabetes, such as insulin, are the most common cause of hypoglycemia.
knowledge_cards.source_span: The most common cause of hypoglycemia is medications used to treat diabetes such as insulin

knowledge_cards.fact_statement: Sweating is a symptom of hypoglycemia associated with insulin use.
knowledge_cards.source_span: A feeling of hunger, sweating, shakiness and weakness may also be present.

knowledge_cards.fact_statement: Shakiness can occur as a symptom of low blood sugar caused by insulin.
knowledge_cards.source_span: A feeling of hunger, sweating, shakiness and weakness may also be present.

knowledge_cards.fact_statement: The aggregation of insulin into fibrillar beta-sheets can cause injection amyloidosis.
knowledge_cards.source_span: This can cause injection amyloidosis, and prevents the storage of insulin for long periods.

knowledge_cards.fact_statement: In some teleost fish, insulin is produced by the Brockmann body.
knowledge_cards.source_span: produced by beta cells of the pancreatic islets in most vertebrates and by the Brockmann body in some teleost fish.

knowledge_cards.fact_statement: Biosynthetic human insulin is manufactured using recombinant DNA technology.
knowledge_cards.source_span: Biosynthetic human insulin (insulin human rDNA, INN) for clinical use is manufactured by recombinant DNA technology.

knowledge_cards.fact_statement: Recombinant insulin is produced in E. coli.
knowledge_cards.source_span: Recombinant insulin is produced either in yeast (usually Saccharomyces cerevisiae) or E. coli.

knowledge_cards.fact_statement: Insulin is produced and stored in the body as a hexamer.
knowledge_cards.source_span: Insulin is produced and stored in the body as a hexamer (a unit of six insulin molecules)
